newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin says French left compromise possible on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Jospin says French left compromise possible on EMU.

text.p: French opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Tuesday he believed a compromise was possible between his party's support for a single European currency and the Communists' demand for a new referendum.

Differences over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) are the main source of discord on the French left in the run-up to the 1998 general election in which it hopes to oust Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government.

"I think there can be an agreement on the left and I think the conditions we have set for moving to the single currency are a responsible and positive approach to this deadline," Jospin said in a France Inter radio interview.
He said the basis for a compromise could be a commitment to hold a vote in both houses of parliament before France enters a single currency, due to be launched in January 1999.
Germany has agreed to hold such a parliamentary vote before switching to the euro, but France, where the legislature is weaker and the executive stronger, has made no such commitment.

The issue has divided the pro-European Socialist and Radical Socialist parties from the anti-EMU Communists and Citizens' Movement -- a small Eurosceptical party led by former socialist defence minister Jean-Pierre Chevenement.

Jospin recalled the Socialists' conditions for accepting EMU included the participation of Italy and Spain from the outset and the establishment of an "economic government" as a political counterweight to the independent European central bank.
He ruled out a referendum on monetary union, saying the French people had already voted in favour of a single currency in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty.

"It would not be normal for France to take its decision on moving to the single currency without the legitimate authorities -- that is parliament in particular -- being involved in this decision," Jospin said.

"That is a path to explore with (Communist leader) Robert Hue and Jean-Pierre Chevenement," he said. "But they must not think they can make us turn our backs on our own positions, and if there were no agreement on the middle course I suggest, then the French people will have to decide in the 1998 general election."
